record.paper_title: Chapter 15: Open Questions and Future Directions in Titan Science
record.context_brief: Availability of phosphorus and sulfur chemistry
record.original_question: What phosphorus- and sulfur-bearing compounds are available for chemistry on Titan, in the atmosphere or on the surface, and can improved astronomical, remote-sensing, or Dragonfly mass-spectrometer measurements detect these CHNOPS elements that are significant for astrobiology and geochemistry despite prior null searches for hydrogen sulfide, carbon sulfide, and phosphine?

evidence.quote: 16) What is the availability of P and S compounds for chemistry?
Six elements are considered the most vital for life on Earth: H, C, N, O, P and S (’CHNOPS’), together constituting 98% of living matter (Cockell et al., 2016).
Searches have been made for atmospheric hydrogen sulfide, carbon sulfide and phosphine with null result so far (Nixon et al., 2013; Teanby et al., 2018).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Saturn's moon Titan possesses a dense N2/CH4 atmosphere with rich organic photochemistry and a surface containing liquid hydrocarbon lakes, water-ice bedrock, and organic sediments. The six elements H, C, N, O, P, S (often abbreviated CHNOPS) are regarded as central to terrestrial biochemistry, comprising roughly 98% of living matter on Earth. To date, remote-sensing searches for the simple phosphorus- and sulfur-bearing molecules H2S, CS, and PH3 in Titan's atmosphere have yielded only non-detections (upper limits).

Determine the inventory and abundances of phosphorus- and sulfur-bearing compounds available for chemistry on Titan, both in the atmosphere and on/within the surface. Specifically:

(a) Identify which P-bearing and S-bearing molecular species (gas-phase, aerosol-bound, or surface-deposited) are expected from photochemical, exogenic (meteoritic/cometary delivery), and cryovolcanic/endogenic sources, and estimate their steady-state abundances and spatial distributions.

(b) Determine whether improved astronomical observations (e.g., ALMA, JWST), future remote-sensing instruments, or in situ mass-spectrometric measurements by a Titan lander/rotorcraft platform can detect these species at the predicted abundance levels, and quantify the detection thresholds required.

(c) Assess the implications of the resulting CHNOPS inventory for prebiotic chemistry, astrobiology, and surface geochemistry on Titan.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as one of the open future-research questions in Titan science. As of 2026, atmospheric searches for H2S, CS, and PH3 on Titan continue to yield only upper limits, and the in situ CHNOPS inventory awaits the Dragonfly mission (currently planned for arrival in the mid-2030s). No publication has comprehensively answered the question, so it remains open.

status_evidence.title: Dragonfly mission overview (NASA/JHUAPL)
status_evidence.snippet: Dragonfly is a rotorcraft lander mission to Titan with a mass spectrometer (DraMS) intended to characterize Titan's surface chemistry, scheduled for launch in 2028 and arrival in the 2030s.
status_evidence.claim: In situ CHNOPS measurements on Titan await Dragonfly arrival in the 2030s, so the question is not yet answered.

status_evidence.title: Nixon et al., upper limits on Titan trace species
status_evidence.snippet: Searches for H2S, CS, and PH3 in Titan's atmosphere yielded null detections with upper-limit constraints.
status_evidence.claim: Phosphorus and sulfur species searches in Titan's atmosphere have so far given only upper limits.
